newsitem.title: USA: U.S. economic upswing seen continuing through 1998.
newsitem.headline: U.S. economic upswing seen continuing through 1998.

text.p: The nearly six-year-old U.S. economic expansion shows no signs of ending and is expected to last at least through the end of 1998, according to a survey of leading private economists released Thursday.
The Blue Chip survey of some 50 economists showed that on average they expect the economy to grow by 2.3 percent this year and 2.1 percent next. It grew 2.5 percent last year.
The 68-month-old economic expansion is already the third longest since the Second World War, surpassed only by the 106-month recovery in the 1960s and the 92-month upswing in the 1980s.
"Central to the consensus forecast of continued economic expansion is the expectation that inflation will remain modest," said the survey published by Alexandria, Va.-based Capitol Publications.
"As long as inflation remains tame, the Federal Reserve is unlikely to raise interest rates," it added.
According to the survey, the economists on average expect consumer price inflation of 2.9 percent this year and 3 percent next. Consumer prices rose about 3 percent in 1996.

Unemployment is forecast to edge up to 5.5 percent by the middle of this year and hold at that level. The unemployment rate in November was 5.4 percent, and the government issues its December jobs report on Friday.
